title.en: The Trials of Entry into the Fianna

region.en: Almhuin (Hill of Allen), Co. Kildare, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭基爾代爾郡艾倫山

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. II, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn's Household chapter preserves the Fianna's warrior code: no cattle by oppression, no refusal of any asker, no retreat before nine fighters — and the fearsome trials of entry: a man half-buried in a hole warding nine spears thrown at once, a hair-plaited run through the woods, a leap and a stoop at speed, and a thorn drawn out with the nail while running. Among the household the sweetest was Cnu Deireoil the Little Nut, come out of the Sidhe.
summary.zh: 菲亞納戰士法典載於本章：不強奪牛隻、不拒任何求助者、九敵之前不後退；入會試煉嚴酷——半身入土擋九矛齊射、辮髮疾奔林間不被追及、疾奔中跨越與俯身、以指甲拔除腳上荊棘。家臣中最甜美者為出自仙族的「小堅果」克努·迪爾奧爾。

sensitivity.note: This is a charter of the fianna warrior institution (ethics + initiation ordeals), a ritual-origin item under the project taxonomy rather than a narrative episode. Pin at Almhuin, Finn's seat.

passages.text: The number of the Fianna of Ireland at that time was seven score and ten chief men, every one of them having three times nine fighting men under him. And every man of them was bound to three things: to take no cattle by oppression, not to refuse any man as to cattle or riches, and no one of them to fall back before nine fighting men. There was no man taken into the Fianna until his tribe and his kindred would give securities for him; and there was no man taken till he knew the twelve books of poetry. And before any man was taken, he would be put into a deep hole in the ground up to his middle, having his shield and a hazel rod in his hand, and nine men would go the length of ten furrows from him and would cast their spears at him at the one time — and if he got a wound from one of them, he was not thought fit to join the Fianna.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: And after that again, his hair would be fastened up, and he put to run through the woods of Ireland, and the Fianna following after him, only the length of a branch between themselves and himself when they started; and if they came up with him and wounded him, or if his spears trembled in his hand, or if a branch of a tree undid the plaiting of his hair, or if he cracked a dry stick under his foot running, he was not let join them. And they would not take him among them till he had made a leap over a stick the height of himself, and stooped under one the height of his knee, and taken a thorn out from his foot with his nail, running his fastest. But if he had done all these things, he was of Finn's people. And of all his musicians the one Finn thought most of was Cnu Deireoil, the Little Nut, that came to him from the Sidhe: a small man about four feet in height, light yellow hair hanging to his waist, playing music on his harp that had no fault in it, come out of the place of the Sidhe in Slieve-nam-ban where ale is drunk and made; and there was never any music heard on earth but his was better.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Birth of Bran and Sceolan
title.zh: 布蘭與斯克奧蘭之誕生

region.zh: 愛爾蘭戈爾韋費爾古斯港

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. III, eBook #14465

summary.en: Jealous of Iollan Eachtach's marriage to her mortal rival, the fairy Uchtdealb of the Fair Breast changes Tuiren into a hound and entrusts her, pregnant, to Fergus Fionnliath — the most dog-hating man in the world — who learns to love hounds through her. Iollan pledges lifelong fidelity to the fairy to win Tuiren's restoration, and the two whelps born in hound-shape are raised by Finn: Bran and Sceolan, who have human wits and will never be without fault.
summary.zh: 因妒忌伊奧蘭娶凡女蒂倫，仙女烏克特戴爾布將蒂倫化為母犬，託付給世上最恨狗的費爾古斯·芬利亞——他卻因她而愛上狗。伊奧蘭向仙女起誓終身不負，換回蒂倫人形；犬身所誕二犬被芬恩撫養——布蘭與斯克奧蘭，具人類心智而無一瑕疵。

sensitivity.note: Etiology of Finn's two great hounds (their names recur in birth-tales of Oisin); transformation-by-druid-rod tag from the fairy's hazel wand. Fergus Fionnliath's dog-hatred cured is a comic annex to the charm.

passages.text: Before Iollan Eachtach made his marriage with Tuiren, Finn's mother's sister, he had a sweetheart of the Sidhe, Uchtdealb of the Fair Breast; and great jealousy came on her when she knew he had taken a wife. She took the appearance of Finn's woman-messenger, came to the house where Tuiren was, and said: "Finn sends health and long life to you, queen, and he bids you to make a great feast; and come with me now till I speak a few words with you, for there is hurry on me." Tuiren went out with her, and when they were away from the house the woman of the Sidhe took out her dark Druid rod from under her cloak and gave her a blow of it that changed her into a hound, the most beautiful that was ever seen. Then she went on, bringing the hound with her, to the house of Fergus Fionnliath, king of the harbour of Gallimh, and it is the way Fergus was, he was the most unfriendly man to dogs in the whole world.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. III; not verbatim.

passages.text: Uchtdealb said to him: "Finn wishes you life and health, Fergus, and he says to you to take good care of his hound till he comes himself; and mind her well, for she is with young." Fergus said: "I wonder at that message, for Finn knows well there is not in the world a man has less liking for dogs than myself. But for all that I will not refuse Finn the first time he sent a hound to me." And when he brought the hound out to try her, she was the best he ever knew, and she never saw the wild creature she would not run down; and Fergus took a great liking for hounds from that out. When her time came she gave birth to two whelps. Iollan, called on for the pledge he had given the Fianna, went to the hill where Uchtdealb was, and promised to keep her as his sweetheart to the end of his life if she would free him from the danger; and she went to the house of Fergus Fionnliath and brought Tuiren away and put her own shape on her again, and gave her up to Finn. And as to the two whelps, they stopped always with Finn, and the names he gave them were Bran and Sceolan.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. III; not verbatim.

title.en: Sadbh the Fawn and the Finding of Oisin
title.zh: 雌鹿莎芙與歐辛的發現

region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡古爾班山

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. IV, eBook #14465

summary.en: A beautiful fawn stops before Finn's hounds and lies on the grass to be licked by Bran and Sceolan; at Almhuin she becomes Sadbh, a woman changed into a deer for refusing the love of the Dark Druid. Finn loves and weds her, but a false likeness lures her from the dun and a hazel rod turns her back to a fawn. Seven years later, hounds penned in a ring on Beinn Gulbain reveal a naked wild boy — the son Sadbh bore — whom Bran and Sceolan play about like their own: Oisin, the maker of poems.
summary.zh: 一頭美麗母鹿在芬恩獵犬前止步，臥於草上任布蘭與斯克奧蘭舔撫；至艾倫山她化回莎芙——因拒絕黑德魯伊之愛而被變為雌鹿。芬恩娶她為妻，然幻影誘她出堡，榛杖將她復化為鹿。七年後，古爾班山上獵犬圍困一赤裸野童——莎芙所生之子。布蘭與斯克奧蘭如親族般親近他：此人即詩人歐辛。

sensitivity.note: The Sadbh-Oisin birth tale is the Fenian cycle's charter of wild-child adoption and of Finn's paternal line; the deception motif (false likeness) is a standard fairy abduction pattern. Pin at Beinn Gulbain, where the boy was found.

passages.text: It happened one time Finn and his men were coming back from the hunting, a beautiful fawn started up before them, and they followed after it, men and dogs, till at last they were all tired and fell back, all but Finn himself and Bran and Sceolan. And suddenly as they were going through a valley, the fawn stopped and lay down on the smooth grass, and Bran and Sceolan came up with it, and they did not harm it at all, but went playing about it, licking its neck and its face. At Almhuin, when Finn was alone late that evening, a beautiful young woman having a rich dress came before him, and she told him it was she herself was the fawn: "It is for refusing the love of Fear Doirche, the Dark Druid of the Men of Dea, I was put in this shape, and through the length of three years I have lived the life of a wild deer in a far part of Ireland, and I am hunted like a wild deer. But a serving-man of the Dark Druid took pity on me and said that if I was once within the dun of the Fianna of Ireland, the Druid would have no more power over me. And I was safe with Bran and Sceolan, for they have human wits, and they knew my nature to be like their own."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. IV; not verbatim.

passages.text: Finn gave her his love and took her as his wife, and so great was his love for her he gave up his hunting and all the things he used to take pleasure in. But the men of Lochlann came against Ireland, and while Finn was away fighting, a likeness of himself and of Bran and of Sceolan appeared before the dun, and Sadbh came out of the house and would not listen to them, but went running out towards the shadow with its arms stretched out to her. No sooner did she touch it than she gave a great cry, and the shadow lifted up a hazel rod, and on the moment it was a fawn was standing on the grass; the two hounds the shadow had with him took her by the throat and dragged her back to him, and then woman and fawn and Druid were not to be seen. Seven years later Finn and his chief men were hunting on the sides of Beinn Gulbain, and the hounds went into some narrow place; and in a ring of the five hounds of Finn was a young boy, naked, with long hair and high looks, that Bran and Sceolan whined and licked about. Little by little he told them all he could remember of a deer he loved, his mother, that a dark-looking man spoke to softly and then in anger, and the last time struck her with a hazel rod and forced her to follow him. And the name the Fianna gave him was Oisin, and it is he was their maker of poems, and their good fighter afterwards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. IV; not verbatim.

title.en: Caoilte's Rabble and the Ransom of Finn
title.zh: 卡爾特之「烏合群」與芬恩的贖身

region.en: Teamhair (Hill of Tara), Co. Meath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡塔拉王丘

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: The High King holds Finn prisoner at Tara for the Fianna's rebellion, and Caoilte avenges him with fire and slaughter until he can slip into the palace disguised as a servant. The king's impossible ransom — a mated couple of every wild creature in Ireland — Caoilte actually fulfils, herding birds and beasts and the very pigs of the son of Lir through the whole island; but at the last all the creatures scatter from Tara, and the people name the horde "Caoilte's Rabble."
summary.zh: 因菲亞納起事，至高王囚芬恩於塔拉；卡爾特縱火屠戮復仇，後喬裝僕役潛入宮中。國王索不可能之贖金——愛爾蘭所有野獸各一對——卡爾特竟真的橫越全島聚齊百獸，連利爾之子的豬也帶來；然而芬恩一獲自由，獸群四散，人稱此群為「卡爾特的烏合群」。

sensitivity.note: The census-of-creatures episode is the Fenian analogue of Noah's ark and of Herakles' herculean labours — the impossible task ransom. Duplicate tag 'sacred-kingship' appears only once in the motif list per schema rules; kept once. Pin at Tara.

passages.text: Another time Caoilte brought Finn out of Teamhair, where he was kept by force by the High King, because of some rebellion the Fianna had stirred up. When Caoilte heard Finn had been brought away to Teamhair, he went out to avenge him: the first he killed was Cuireach, a king of Leinster that had a great name, and after that he made a great rout through Ireland, bringing sorrow into every house for the sake of Finn, killing a man in every place, and setting fire to the fields. And when he came to Teamhair he took the clothes off the door-keeper, and left his own worn sword in the king's sheath and took the king's sword that had great power in it, and went into the palace in the disguise of a servant. When evening came he held the candle at the king's feast, and the king said: "You will wonder at what I tell you, Finn, that the two eyes of Caoilte are in my candlestick." "Do not say that," said Finn, "and do not put reproach on my people; for it is a high mind Caoilte has, and he only does high deeds, and he would not stand serving with a candle for all the gold of the whole world."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Caoilte gave out a high sorrowful lament as he served the king with drink, and when the king knew him, he spoke out: "Tell me what way I can get freedom for my master." "There is no way but by doing one thing you can never do. If you can bring me together a couple of all the wild creatures of Ireland, I will give up your master to you then." Caoilte made no delay, but went through the whole of Ireland: two ravens from Fiodh da Bheann, two wild ducks from Loch na Seillein, two foxes from Slieve Cuilinn, two swans from blue Dobhran, two eagles from the Carraig of the stones, two deer from Sith Buidhe, two peacocks from Magh Mell, two cats from the Cave of Cruachan, and two pigs of the pigs of the son of Lir — and a horse and a mare of the beautiful horses of Manannan. When he brought them to Teamhair the king gave him a house with nine doors to put them up in for the night, and they raised a loud screech together through fifty openings, trying to make their escape. And when he brought out his troop, the name the people gave them was "Caoilte's Rabble." But all the profit the King of Ireland got from them was to see them together for that one time; for no sooner did Finn get his freedom than the whole of them scattered here and there, and no two of them went by the same road out of Teamhair.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

title.en: Finn's Advice to a Young Champion
title.zh: 芬恩對年輕戰士的訓誡

region.en: Corraig Conluain, Slieve Bladhma, Co. Tipperary, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭蒂珀雷里郡布洛馬山科雷格·康盧因

texts.period: Fenian cycle, medieval Irish tradition (speculum principis material); Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book I, ch. V, eBook #14465

summary.en: Lugaidh's Son, sluggish and quarrelsome among the Fianna, is nearly cast out; Finn gives him the famous advice of a champion — be quiet in a great man's house and surly in the narrow pass; give two-thirds of your gentleness to women, children, and poets; never promise what you cannot carry out, nor forsake a man under your protection. The advice stays with him, and he wins a great name among the poets of Ireland and Alban — and the love of Aoife, wife of the King of Alban, who sails to Ireland for him.
summary.zh: 盧蓋德之子在菲亞納中疏懶好鬥，幾被逐出；芬恩授以戰士經典訓誡——豪門之宅當謙、狹路之險當橫；把三分之二的溫柔留給婦孺與詩人；不作力不能及之諾，不棄受你庇護之人。此訓誡永伴其身，令他名揚愛爾蘭與阿爾巴詩壇——並贏得遠航來愛爾蘭的阿爾巴王后艾菲之愛。

sensitivity.note: The advice to Lugaidh's Son is a Teagusc na n-ingeh (conduct-instruction) embedded in narrative — Fenian wisdom literature rather than a plot episode; tagged parable-teaching deliberately.

passages.text: Lugaidh's Son, that was of Finn's blood, was put into Finn's arms as a child, and reared by Duban's daughter, that had reared eight hundred fighting men of the Fianna. He stopped through the length of a year with the Fianna, but he was someway sluggish through all that time, so that under his leading not more than nine of the Fianna got to kill so much as a boar or a deer; and along with that, he used to beat both his servants and his hounds. At last the three battalions of the Fianna made their complaint to Finn: "Make your choice now, will you have us with you, or will you have Lugaidh's Son by himself."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then Finn gave him his advice, and it is what he said: "If you have a mind to be a good champion, be quiet in a great man's house; be surly in the narrow pass. Do not beat your hound without a cause; do not bring a charge against your wife without having knowledge of her guilt; do not hurt a fool in fighting, for he is without his wits. Let two-thirds of your gentleness be showed to women and to little children that are creeping on the floor, and to men of learning that make the poems, and do not be rough with the common people. Do not threaten or speak big words, for it is a shameful thing to speak stiffly unless you can carry it out afterwards. Do not forsake your lord so long as you live; do not give up any man that puts himself under your protection for all the treasures of the world. Do not refuse to share your meat; hold fast to your arms till the hard fight is well ended; and with that follow after gentleness." That advice stayed always with Lugaidh's Son, and he changed his ways, and after a while he got a great name among the poets of Ireland and of Alban. And Aoife, daughter of the King of Lochlann, wife of Mal, King of Alban, heard the great praise the poets were giving him and set her love on him, and came over the manes of the sea to Ireland with her nine foster-sisters to look for him; and when her husband Mal came to avenge her with three battalions, it was Mal fell by Lugaidh's Son at the last, and Aoife stood on a hill near by as long as the battle lasted.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book I, ch. V; not verbatim.
